categories.label: Traditional Jazz / Dixieland
categories.description: The earliest jazz style, originating in New Orleans. Drawing on ragtime and brass-band vocabulary, it's defined by collective improvisation (polyphony), with several horns improvising simultaneously.

categories.label: Swing (Big Band)
categories.description: Jazz as dance music, led by large big bands. Count Basie and Duke Ellington carried popular music's mainstream with polished arrangements and propulsive rhythm.

categories.label: Vocal Jazz
categories.description: A lineage rooted in swing-era big-band singers, delivering standards with scat and sophisticated phrasing. Established by Ella Fitzgerald and Sarah Vaughan, among others.

categories.label: Bebop
categories.description: A breakaway from swing's dance-music role, pursuing improvisation through fast tempos, complex chord changes, and intricate phrasing. Centered on Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie.

categories.label: Latin Jazz
categories.description: A genre fusing Afro-Cuban rhythms with bebop's vocabulary. It developed out of Dizzy Gillespie's collaboration with Chano Pozo.

categories.label: Cool Jazz / West Coast Jazz
categories.description: A style favoring restrained tone and chamber-music-like arrangement in contrast to bebop's intensity. Carried largely by Miles Davis's work and the West Coast scene.

categories.label: Hard Bop
categories.description: A style that brought the earthiness of blues and gospel back into bebop. Led by Art Blakey & the Jazz Messengers and Horace Silver.

categories.label: Soul Jazz
categories.description: A style that deepened hard bop's gospel/R&B elements, built around the organ and driven by a buoyant groove. Jimmy Smith's organ trios are the archetype.

categories.label: Modal Jazz
categories.description: A method building improvisation on scales (modes) rather than chord changes. Established by Miles Davis's "Kind of Blue" and John Coltrane's exploration.

categories.label: Free Jazz (Avant-Garde)
categories.description: A style freed from tonality, meter, and existing chord progressions, pursuing collective improvisation and sound itself. Pioneered by Ornette Coleman and Cecil Taylor.

categories.label: Post-Bop
categories.description: An eclectic style that absorbed modal jazz and free jazz's vocabulary while retaining hard bop's song structure. Wayne Shorter and Herbie Hancock's work is representative.

categories.label: Jazz Fusion
categories.description: A genre incorporating rock and funk beats and electric instruments. Sparked by Miles Davis's "Bitches Brew" and developed further by Weather Report, among others.

categories.label: Smooth Jazz
categories.description: An instrumental style pushing fusion toward pop-friendly accessibility. Popular on adult-contemporary radio.

categories.label: Acid Jazz / Nu Jazz
categories.description: A club-born style pairing house and hip-hop beats with jazz and funk grooves. US3 and Groove Collective are representative.

categories.label: Other
categories.description: Artists that don't clearly fit the above categories, or that cross multiple styles.
